topics.intro: This topic covers the real number system and binary operations: how to evaluate a new rule, test its properties, and find identities and inverses.

sections.title: The real number system
body: Numbers are sorted into sets. **N** (natural numbers) are the counting numbers 1, 2, 3, ... **Z** (integers) are positive and negative whole numbers, and zero.
**Q** (rational numbers) are numbers a/b with a, b integers and b ≠ 0. Their decimals terminate or recur: −5, 5/8 = 0.625, 2/3 = 0.666...
**I** (irrational numbers) cannot be written as a/b. Their decimals never terminate or recur: √2, √3, π, e.
**R** (real numbers) are all the rational and all the irrational numbers: every point on the number line.
The sets fit inside one another: **N ⊂ Z ⊂ Q ⊂ R**. The irrationals are the part of R that lies outside Q.

**The number line.** Put 0 at the centre, positive numbers to the right and negative numbers to the left. Each real number matches exactly one point on the line, and each point matches one real number.
keyPoints: N ⊂ Z ⊂ Q ⊂ R; the irrationals lie in R but outside Q.
Rational decimals terminate or recur.

sections.title: Laws of arithmetic
body: For any integers a, b and c (these laws also hold for all real numbers):
**Commutative:** a + b = b + a and ab = ba.
**Associative:** (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) and (ab)c = a(bc).
**Distributive:** a(b + c) = ab + ac.
These are the laws we test when we meet new operations in the next sections. Subtraction, for example, is **not** commutative: 5 − 3 ≠ 3 − 5.
keyPoints: Commutative: swap the order. Associative: regroup. Distributive: a(b + c) = ab + ac.

sections.title: Binary operations
body: A **binary operation** is a rule that combines two elements to give one result, such as + or ×. New rules are written with symbols like ∗, ∆ or ∘.
**To evaluate one, substitute the two numbers into the rule, keeping their order.**
**Example 4.3.** If a ⊙ b = the smaller of a and b, then 4 ⊙ 9 = 9 ⊙ 4 = 4 and 11 ⊙ 3 = 3.

sections.title: Properties of a binary operation
body: To describe a binary operation we test five properties (for all a, b, c in the set).
**Closed:** a ∗ b is always in the set. **Commutative:** a ∗ b = b ∗ a. **Associative:** (a ∗ b) ∗ c = a ∗ (b ∗ c).
**Identity e:** a ∗ e = e ∗ a = a, with the same e for every a. **Inverse of a:** a ∗ a⁻¹ = a⁻¹ ∗ a = e.
To **disprove** a property, one counter-example is enough. To **prove** it, use letters.
**Example 4.9 (closure).** a ∗ b = a + b − 2 on S = {2, 3, 5, 7}. Fill in the table of results. Results such as 4 are not in S, so S is **not closed**.
keyPoints: Closed, commutative, associative, identity, inverse.

sections.title: Closure and number sets
body: Closure depends on the set as well as the rule. Check the results in the **whole table**, or look for one result that falls outside the set.
**Example 4.14.** a ∆ b = a + b − ab on T = {0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. T is not closed (5 ∆ 6 = −19).
**Example 4.13.** a ∇ b = (a + b)/(ab) on the non-zero rationals. It is **not closed**, since 1 ∇ (−1) = 0/(−1) = 0, and 0 is not a non-zero rational.
Think of the number sets. The natural numbers are closed under + and ×, but not under − (3 − 5 = −2) or ÷ (1 ÷ 2 is not natural).

sections.title: Commutative and associative tests
body: **Example 4.12.** For a ∆ b = ab + a, take a = 1, b = 1, c = 2. (1 ∆ 1) ∆ 2 = 2 ∆ 2 = **6**, but 1 ∆ (1 ∆ 2) = 1 ∆ 3 = **4**. So it is **not associative**.

**Example 4.13.** a ∇ b = (a + b)/(ab) on the non-zero rationals is commutative, because the rule is the same when a and b swap. It is not associative: (1 ∇ 1) ∇ 2 = 2 ∇ 2 = 1, but 1 ∇ (1 ∇ 2) = 1 ∇ 3/2 = **5/3**.
**Added practice.** On the real numbers, a ∗ b = a + b − 3. It is commutative, since a + b − 3 = b + a − 3. It is associative: (a ∗ b) ∗ c = a + b + c − 6 = a ∗ (b ∗ c).
keyPoints: Associative test: compare (a ∗ b) ∗ c with a ∗ (b ∗ c).

sections.title: Identity and inverse
body: To find the **identity** e, solve a ∗ e = a. To find the **inverse** y of a, solve a ∗ y = e.

**Examples 4.19 and 4.23.** a ∗ b = a + b + 2ab. From a + e + 2ae = a we get e(1 + 2a) = 0, so **e = 0**. From a + y + 2ay = 0 the inverse is **y = −a/(1 + 2a)**. The element −1/2 has no inverse. The inverses of 2 and 3 are −2/5 and −3/7.
**Example 4.22.** For a ∆ b = (3a + 3b − 2)/3, solving a ∆ e = a gives **e = 2/3**.
**Example 4.14.** a ∆ b = a + b − ab: the identity is 0, and the inverse of 2 is 2.
**Added practice.** For a ∗ b = a + b − 3: the identity is 3, and the inverse of a is **6 − a**, so the inverse of 5 is 1.
keyPoints: Identity: solve a ∗ e = a.
Inverse: solve a ∗ y = e.

sections.title: More identity and inverse examples
body: Here are three more rules to practise on (**Examples 4.25 to 4.28**).
**m + n + 10.** The identity is **−10**. The inverse of a is **−20 − a**, so the inverses of 2 and −5 are **−22** and **−15**.
**p + q + √2.** The identity is **−√2**. The inverse of a is **−a − 2√2**. The inverse of 2√2 is **−4√2**, and (√2 − 1) ∗ (√2 + 1) = 2√2 + √2 = **3√2**.
**p + q − 2.** The identity is 2, the inverse of a is 4 − a, and it is associative: both bracketings give **p + q + r − 4**.
keyPoints: Same method every time: solve a ∗ e = a, then a ∗ y = e.

sections.title: What is a set?
body: A **set** is a well-defined collection of objects: for any object, we can say clearly whether it belongs. Its members (**elements**) go in curly brackets, and repeats are not counted. x ∈ A means "x belongs to A"; x ∉ A means it does not.
**Describing a set.** You can list the members, P = {2, 3, 5, 7, 11}; state a property, P = {primes less than 12}; or use set-builder notation, P = {x : x is prime and x < 12}.
**Examples.** In set-builder notation, the odd numbers greater than 30 are {x : x is odd and x > 30}. For G = {2, 3, 5, 6, 9}, n(G) = **5**.
Two sets with the same members are the same set: {2, 3, 5} = {5, 2, 3}.
keyPoints: A set is a well-defined collection; repeats are not counted.

sections.title: Sets: key terms
body: **Finite / infinite:** the count of elements ends / never ends. {1, 2, 3} is finite; {1, 2, 3, ...} is infinite.
**Empty set ∅:** no elements; n(∅) = 0. Example: {integers x : 2 < x < 3}.
**Subset A ⊆ B:** every element of A is in B. Example: {2, 5, 8} ⊆ {1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8}.
**Equal sets:** exactly the same elements. **Equivalent sets:** the same number of elements, for example {2, 3, 5} and {11, 12, 13}.

**Universal set U:** everything under discussion, such as all integers. **Complement A′:** the elements of U not in A. If U = integers and A = odd, then A′ = even. **Cardinality n(A):** the number of elements; n({a, m, b, d, h}) = 5.
**Take care:** ⊆ links a set to a set, while ∈ links an element to a set. The empty set is a subset of every set. These notes use ⊆ for "subset of" (your lecturer may write ⊂).
**Venn diagrams for 'all ... are ...'.** "All scientists are introverts; all introverts are anti-social" is drawn as three circles, one inside another: scientists ⊆ introverts ⊆ anti-social.
keyPoints: ⊆ links sets; ∈ links an element to a set.

body: **Intersection A ∩ B:** in both A and B (key word: and). **Union A ∪ B:** in A or B or both (or). **Complement A′:** not in A (not).

sections.title: Counting with two sets
body: **Counting rule** (subtracting stops the overlap being counted twice): **n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)**.

**Example 3.13.** In a survey, 10 students like Chemistry only, 15 like both Chemistry and Physics, 11 like Physics only and 4 like neither. So 25 like Chemistry, 21 like exactly one subject, 36 like Chemistry or Physics, and 40 were interviewed.
**Example 3.15.** x candidates take Geography, 3x take Physics, 6 take both and there are 46 in all (each takes at least one). Then 46 = x + 3x − 6, so **x = 13**.

**Exercise 3.2, question 2.** Of 50 traders, 30 sell garri and 40 sell rice, and each sells at least one. 50 = 30 + 40 − n(both), so **20** sell both. **Question 11.** In a class of 42, 26 take Mathematics and 28 take Chemistry, and each takes at least one: 42 = 26 + 28 − n(both), so **12** take both.
keyPoints: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

sections.title: Laws of sets
body: **Commutative:** A ∪ B = B ∪ A and A ∩ B = B ∩ A. **Associative:** (A ∪ B) ∪ C = A ∪ (B ∪ C) and (A ∩ B) ∩ C = A ∩ (B ∩ C).
**Distributive:** A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C) and A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C). **Absorption:** A ∪ (A ∩ B) = A and A ∩ (A ∪ B) = A. **Idempotent:** A ∪ A = A and A ∩ A = A.
**De Morgan:** (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′. **Complement:** A ∪ A′ = U and A ∩ A′ = ∅.
**Identity:** A ∪ ∅ = A and A ∩ U = A. **Domination:** A ∪ U = U and A ∩ ∅ = ∅.
Also U′ = ∅, ∅′ = U and (A′)′ = A. If A ⊆ B and B ⊆ C, then A ⊆ C. If A ⊆ B and A ⊆ C, then A ⊆ B ∩ C.
keyPoints: De Morgan swaps ∪ and ∩ when taking a complement.

sections.title: Splitting a fraction: the idea and the forms
body: Partial fractions means splitting one fraction into simpler ones. **If the top's degree is not smaller than the bottom's, divide first.** Then factorise the bottom and choose the form.
**Factor (ax + b):** write A/(ax + b).
**Factor (ax + b)²:** write A/(ax + b) + B/(ax + b)².
**Factor (x² + k), k > 0:** write (Ax + B)/(x² + k).
**Factor (x² + k)²:** write (Ax + B)/(x² + k) + (Cx + D)/(x² + k)².
Find the constants by substituting convenient values of x, or by comparing coefficients.
keyPoints: Divide first if the top's degree is not smaller than the bottom's.
One term for each power of a repeated factor; a linear top over a quadratic factor.

sections.title: Improper fractions: divide first
body: When the top's degree is not smaller than the bottom's, divide first. The quotient is a polynomial; the remainder is split into partial fractions.

(x² + 5x − 10)/(x² − 4x − 12). Here x² − 4x − 12 = (x − 6)(x + 2). Dividing gives 1 with remainder 9x + 2, so the fraction is 1 + (9x + 2)/[(x − 6)(x + 2)]. Then 9x + 2 = A(x + 2) + B(x − 6): x = 6 gives A = 7 and x = −2 gives B = 2. The result is **1 + 7/(x − 6) + 2/(x + 2)**.

topics.intro: This topic counts the ways to arrange or choose things. You will learn permutations (order matters), combinations (order does not), how to count arrangements of letters, and the binomial theorem, which expands powers like (1 + x)⁵.

sections.title: Counting and permutations
body: **The multiplication principle.** If one job can be done in 3 ways and another in 4 ways, the two jobs together can be done in 3 × 4 = 12 ways. Everything in this topic grows from that simple idea.
**Factorial.** n! (say 'n factorial') means n × (n − 1) × … × 2 × 1. So 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120. We define **0! = 1.**

A **permutation** is an **arrangement where order matters.** A selection in which the order of choice is important is a permutation. Arranging **all** n different objects in a row can be done in **n!** ways: the first place has n choices, the second n − 1, and so on. So **ⁿPₙ = n!**

Arranging only **r** of the n objects: the first place has n choices, the second n − 1, down to r choices, so **ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)! = n(n − 1)(n − 2)…(n − r + 1).** Example: ¹⁰P₄ = 10 × 9 × 8 × 7 = **5040.** Also ¹²P₇ = 12 × 11 × 10 × 9 × 8 × 7 × 6 = **3,991,680.**
**Reading ⁿPᵣ backwards.** If ⁿPᵣ = 13 × 12 × 11 × 10 × 9, there are five factors starting from 13, so **n = 13 and r = 5.** If ⁿPᵣ = 20!/(20 − 14)!, compare with n!/(n − r)!: **n = 20 and r = 14.**
keyPoints: ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)! (order matters).

sections.title: Arranging letters, including repeated ones
body: If all the objects are different, they can be arranged in n! ways. So the letters of **PENCIL** (6 different letters) can be arranged in **6! = 720** ways.
If some objects are **identical**, swapping them changes nothing, so we divide. **n!/(p! q! r! …)**, where p, q, r are the numbers of each repeated object.

**CALCULUS** has 8 letters: C appears 2 times, A once, L twice, U twice and S once. So the number of arrangements is **8!/(2! 2! 2!)** = 40320/8 = **5040.** (Check each letter: C, A, L, C, U, L, U, S gives C × 2, L × 2, U × 2.)
Another: BANANA has 6 letters with A three times and N twice, so 6!/(3! 2!) = 720/12 = **60.**
**A good habit.** Write the letter counts first, in a short list, and then write the fraction. Most mistakes come from missing a repeated letter.
keyPoints: All different: n!.

sections.title: Combinations: order does not matter
body: A **combination** is a selection where **order does not matter**. Choosing a committee is a combination: {Ada, Bayo, Chi} is the same committee as {Chi, Ada, Bayo}.
Every group of r objects can be arranged in r! ways. So the number of combinations is the number of permutations divided by r!: **ⁿCᵣ = n!/((n − r)! r!)**.

Example: ⁵C₃ = 5!/(2! 3!) = 120/12 = **10.** And ⁶C₄ = 6!/(2! 4!) = 720/48 = **15.** There is a useful symmetry, **ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ**, because choosing 3 to include is the same as choosing 2 to leave out. So ⁷C₃ = ⁷C₄ = 35.
**Several groups at once.** A committee of 3 boys and 4 girls is chosen from 5 boys and 6 girls. Choose the boys: ⁵C₃ = 10. Choose the girls: ⁶C₄ = 15. Multiply: 10 × 15 = **150.**

The formula in an exam might be given as a 'which is true' question. The correct one is **ⁿCᵣ = n!/((n − r)! r!)**. Be careful with look-alikes where the last factor is n! instead of r!; those are wrong.
keyPoints: ⁿCᵣ = n!/((n − r)! r!). Order does not matter.

sections.title: Inequalities and the number line
body: An equation says two sides are balanced. An **inequality** says one side is bigger or smaller. The symbols are < (less than), ≤ (less than or equal to), > (greater than) and ≥ (greater than or equal to).
**Rule 1.** Adding or subtracting the same number on both sides keeps the sign.
**Rule 2.** Multiplying or dividing both sides by a **positive** number keeps the sign.
**Rule 3.** Multiplying or dividing both sides by a **negative** number **reverses** the sign. For example, 2 < 5 but −2 > −5.
On a number line, an **open circle ○** means the end point is excluded (< or >). A **filled circle ●** means it is included (≤ or ≥).
**Example 1.1(a).** Solve 6x − 3 > 39. Add 3: 6x > 42, so **x > 7** (open circle at 7, arrow to the right).
keyPoints: Multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the sign.
Open circle: end point excluded. Filled circle: included.

Since |x − 5| is positive, |x + 4| ≤ 8|x − 5|. Both sides are non-negative, so we may **square** both sides.
(x + 4)² ≤ 64(x − 5)². So 64(x − 5)² − (x + 4)² ≥ 0, which factorises as (7x − 44)(9x − 36) ≥ 0.
The critical values are 4 and 44/7. The answer is **x ≤ 4 or x ≥ 44/7**.
**Check.** x = 5.5 gives 9.5/0.5 = 19, which is greater than 8, so it is correctly excluded.

sections.title: The triangle inequality
body: For all real numbers x and y: **|x + y| ≤ |x| + |y|**.
**Proof by cases.** (1) x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0: |x + y| = x + y = |x| + |y|. (2) x < 0 and y < 0: |x + y| = −x − y = |x| + |y|.
(3) x ≥ 0 and y < 0: here |x| = x and |y| = −y. If x + y ≥ 0, then |x + y| = x + y = |x| − |y| ≤ |x| + |y|. If x + y < 0, then |x + y| = −x − y = −|x| + |y| ≤ |x| + |y|.
(4) x < 0 and y ≥ 0: swap the names of x and y in case 3. In every case |x + y| ≤ |x| + |y|. ∎
**A shorter proof.** We know −|x| ≤ x ≤ |x| and −|y| ≤ y ≤ |y|. Adding gives −(|x| + |y|) ≤ x + y ≤ |x| + |y|, which says exactly that |x + y| ≤ |x| + |y|. ∎
keyPoints: |x + y| ≤ |x| + |y| for all real x and y.
Shorter proof: add −|x| ≤ x ≤ |x| and −|y| ≤ y ≤ |y|.

**Example Q1.** 2x² − 5x + k = 0 has equal roots when 25 − 8k = 0, so **k = 25/8**.
**Example Q2.** 5x² − 6x − 8 = (5x + 4)(x − 2), so x = **−4/5 or 2**. Completing the square, (x − 3/5)² = 49/25, gives the same roots.

body: If the roots are α and β, then **α + β = −b/a** and **αβ = c/a**. A quadratic with given roots is **x² − (sum)x + (product) = 0**.
You can find new equations without solving the old one. **Example Q3.** The roots of x² − mx + n = 0 are α, β (n ≠ 0). Find the equation with roots α/β² and β/α².
The sum is (α³ + β³)/(αβ)² = m(m² − 3n)/n² and the product is 1/n. So the equation is **n²x² − m(m² − 3n)x + n = 0**.
**Added practice.** For 2x² − 4x + 1 = 0: α + β = 2 and αβ = 1/2, so α² + β² = 4 − 1 = 3. The roots 1/α and 1/β have sum (α + β)/αβ = 4 and product 2, giving **x² − 4x + 2 = 0**.

sections.title: Mathematical induction
body: Induction proves that a statement is true for every positive integer from a starting value. Think of a row of dominoes: if the first falls, and each one knocks over the next, then all of them fall.
**1. Base step:** show the statement is true for the first value (usually n = 1).
**2. Assumption:** suppose it is true for n = k.
**3. Inductive step:** using that assumption, show it is true for n = k + 1.
**4. Conclusion:** so it is true for all n from the first value onwards.
keyPoints: Base step, assumption, inductive step, conclusion.
The inductive step uses the assumption for n = k.

sections.title: Induction: inequalities and divisibility
body: **Example 1.9.** Prove that n² ≥ 2n + 1 for n ≥ 3. For n = 3: 9 ≥ 7, which is true. Assume k² ≥ 2k + 1, where k ≥ 3. Then (k + 1)² = k² + 2k + 1 ≥ 4k + 2. Since 2k > 1, we have 4k + 2 > 2k + 3 = 2(k + 1) + 1. ∎

**Example 1.10.** Prove that n³ − n is divisible by 3. For n = 1 the value is 0, which is divisible by 3. Assume 3 divides k³ − k. Then (k + 1)³ − (k + 1) = (k³ − k) + 3(k² + k). Both parts are divisible by 3, so the sum is too. ∎
**Exercise 1, question 6.** For n³ + 2n, the step adds 3(k² + k + 1) to k³ + 2k.
**Exercise 1, question 7.** For 3^(2n+1) + 2^(n+2): n = 1 gives 35. If f(k) is the expression, f(k + 1) = 2f(k) + 7 × 3^(2k+1).
keyPoints: Divisibility: write f(k + 1) as f(k) plus a multiple of the divisor.
Inequality: build the (k + 1) case from the assumption.

body: **Exercise 1, question 5.** Prove by induction that 1³ + 2³ + ... + n³ = [n(n + 1)/2]².
For n = 1 both sides equal 1. Assume the result for n = k and add (k + 1)³ to both sides. The right side becomes [k(k + 1)/2]² + (k + 1)³ = (k + 1)²(k²/4 + k + 1).
The key step is (k + 1)²(k²/4 + k + 1) = [(k + 1)(k + 2)/2]². That is the formula with n = k + 1. ∎
keyPoints: Add the next term to both sides, then factorise to match the formula for n = k + 1.

sections.title: Induction proves De Moivre's theorem
body: **Example 1.8 (De Moivre's theorem).** Prove that (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ for all positive integers n.
It is clearly true for n = 1. Assume it for n = k. Then, using i² = −1 and the compound-angle formulas:
(cos θ + i sin θ)^(k+1) = (cos kθ + i sin kθ)(cos θ + i sin θ) = (cos kθ cos θ − sin kθ sin θ) + i(sin kθ cos θ + cos kθ sin θ) = cos(k + 1)θ + i sin(k + 1)θ. ∎
You will use this theorem in the Complex Numbers topic.
keyPoints: Assume the result for n = k, multiply by (cos θ + i sin θ), and use the compound-angle formulas.

sections.title: Sequences and series
body: A **sequence** is a list of numbers in a definite order: U₁, U₂, U₃, ..., Uₙ. Uₙ is the **n-th term** (general term). A sequence that ends is **finite**; otherwise it is **infinite**.
A **series** is what you get when you add the terms: **Sₙ = U₁ + U₂ + ... + Uₙ**, written Σ Uᵣ for r from 1 to n. So **Uₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁** for n ≥ 2, and U₁ = S₁.
**Example 2.4.** The sum of r² from r = 1 to 4 is 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 = **30**. The sum of 2ʳ from r = 3 to 7 is 8 + 16 + 32 + 64 + 128 = **248**.
keyPoints: Sₙ = U₁ + U₂ + ... + Uₙ and Uₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁.

sections.title: Arithmetic progression (AP)
body: An **AP** (linear sequence) goes up or down by the same amount each time: the **common difference** d = Uₙ − Uₙ₋₁. Its terms are a, a + d, a + 2d, ...
**Where the sum comes from.** Write the series forwards, then backwards, and add. Each of the n pairs equals 2a + (n − 1)d, so 2Sₙ = n[2a + (n − 1)d].
**Proof by induction.** For n = 1 both sides equal a. Assume the formula for n = k and add the next term, a + kd: S(k+1) = (k/2)[2a + (k − 1)d] + a + kd = ((k + 1)/2)(2a + kd). ∎
**Arithmetic mean.** The mean of two numbers is half their sum. To insert several means between two numbers, make them all part of one AP.
keyPoints: Uₙ = a + (n − 1)d.

**Example 2.6.** The 3rd term is 10, the nth is 8 and the 2nth is 9/2. Find Sₙ. We have a + 2d = 10, a + (n − 1)d = 8 and a + (2n − 1)d = 9/2. These give nd = −7/2, d = −1/2, a = 11, n = 7. So **S₇ = 133/2**.
**Example 2.7.** If Sₙ = n(n + 2), then Uₙ = 2n + 1, so the AP is **3, 5, 7, 9, ...**

**Example 2.8.** Five numbers in AP have sum 25 and squares summing to 165. Call them a − 2d, a − d, a, a + d, a + 2d. Then 5a = 25, so a = 5. Also 5a² + 10d² = 165, so d = ±2. The numbers are **1, 3, 5, 7, 9**.

sections.title: Geometric progression (GP)
body: In a **GP** (exponential sequence) each term is the previous one multiplied by the **common ratio** r: a, ar, ar², ...
**Where the sum comes from.** Sₙ − rSₙ = a − arⁿ, because all the middle terms cancel. (By induction: adding arᵏ to a(1 − rᵏ)/(1 − r) gives a(1 − rᵏ⁺¹)/(1 − r).)
**Geometric mean.** If x, y, z are in GP then y² = xz. To insert n geometric means between x and z (positive), use rⁿ⁺¹ = z/x.
**Sum to infinity.** If |r| < 1, then rⁿ → 0, so the series **converges**: **S∞ = a/(1 − r)**. If a ≠ 0 and |r| ≥ 1, the series **diverges**.
keyPoints: Uₙ = arⁿ⁻¹; Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r).

sections.title: Convergence of series
body: The sum Sₙ of the first n terms is a **partial sum**. If Sₙ approaches a finite limit S, the series **converges** to S. Otherwise it **diverges**.
**Example 2.3.1.** For the sum of 1/[r(r + 1)], the partial sums are 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, 4/5, ... In general Sₙ = n/(n + 1), which approaches **1**.
**Theorem 1.** If a series converges, then Uₙ → 0. Proof: Uₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁ → S − S = 0.
**The reverse is false.** In the harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ..., the terms tend to 0 but the series diverges. So if Uₙ does not tend to 0, the series diverges; if it does, you need another test.
keyPoints: Converges: Sₙ tends to a finite limit.
Uₙ → 0 is necessary for convergence, not sufficient.

sections.title: Tests for series of positive terms
body: **Comparison test.** If Uᵣ ≤ Vᵣ (for large r) and ΣV converges, ΣU converges. If Uᵣ ≥ Vᵣ and ΣV diverges, ΣU diverges.
**Ratio comparison.** If Uᵣ₊₁/Uᵣ ≤ Vᵣ₊₁/Vᵣ and ΣV converges, ΣU converges. If ≥ and ΣV diverges, ΣU diverges.
**d'Alembert's ratio test.** Let K = lim Uᵣ₊₁/Uᵣ. K < 1: converges. K > 1: diverges. K = 1: no conclusion.
**Cauchy's integral test.** If f is positive and decreasing for x ≥ 1 with f(r) = Uᵣ, then ΣU and the integral of f from 1 to ∞ both converge or both diverge.
**Example A.** For Σ r/2ʳ, the ratio is (r + 1)/(2r) → 1/2 < 1, so it **converges**. **Example B.** For Σ 1/r!, the ratio is 1/(r + 1) → 0, so it **converges**.
keyPoints: Ratio test: K < 1 converges, K > 1 diverges, K = 1 no conclusion.

2. 8/9 + 11/27 + 14/81 + ..., with general term (3r + 5)/3^(r+1), **converges** (the ratio tends to 1/3).
3. Σ r/[(r + 1)(2r − 1)] **diverges** (compare with 1/r: the terms behave like 1/(2r)).
4. Σ 1/[2r(r + 1)] **converges** (compare with 1/r²).
5. Σ r!/10ʳ **diverges** (the ratio (r + 1)/10 tends to infinity).

**Example C.** For which x does Σ xⁿ/(1 + xⁿ) converge? (x ≠ −1.) If |x| < 1, the size of the ratio tends to |x| < 1, so it converges absolutely. If |x| > 1, the terms tend to 1, not 0, so it diverges. At x = 1 every term is 1/2, so it diverges. At x = −1 the odd terms are undefined. So it converges for **−1 < x < 1**: an interval centred at 0 with **radius** 1.

sections.title: Alternating series and absolute convergence
body: **Alternating series test.** If the signs alternate, the sizes of the terms decrease, and they tend to 0, the series converges. With a positive first term, **U₁ − U₂ ≤ L ≤ U₁**, where U₁, U₂ are the sizes.
**Example D.** 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − 1/4 + ... meets all the conditions, so it converges, with **1/2 ≤ L ≤ 1**.

**Absolute and conditional convergence.** If Σ|Uᵣ| converges, then ΣUᵣ is **absolutely convergent** (and so convergent). If ΣUᵣ converges but Σ|Uᵣ| does not, it is **conditionally convergent**. Example D is conditionally convergent.
keyPoints: Alternating, decreasing, tending to 0: converges.
Absolutely convergent means Σ|Uᵣ| converges.

sections.title: Maclaurin series
body: A Maclaurin series writes a function as a sum of powers of x. All derivatives at 0 must exist, and the series equals the function only where it converges to it.
**Method:** differentiate several times, put x = 0 in each result, then substitute into the formula.
For sin 3x, replace x by 3x in the sine series: 3x − 9x³/2 + 81x⁵/40 − ...
